Let
\[
\Delta=\sqrt{t^4-t^2+1},\qquad
x=\frac{1+t^2-\Delta}{3}.
\]
Then the largest possible volume is
\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{3}\bigl(x(1-x)(t^2-x)\bigr)^{1/4}}.
\]

To prove this, use oriented face-area vectors. For a tetrahedron, let \(P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4\) be the outward normal vectors whose lengths are the corresponding face areas. Then
\[
P_1+P_2+P_3+P_4=0.
\]
Conversely, any four noncoplanar vectors with this sum and prescribed lengths are the face-area vectors of a unique tetrahedron up to translation.

If three edges from one vertex are \(u,v,w\), set
\[
X=\frac12 v\times w,\qquad Y=\frac12 w\times u,\qquad Z=\frac12 u\times v.
\]
Then the fourth face-area vector is \(-(X+Y+Z)\), and
\[
\det(X,Y,Z)=\frac{(u\cdot(v\times w))^2}{8}.
\]
Since \(u\cdot(v\times w)=6V\),
\[
V=\frac{\sqrt{2\,|\det(X,Y,Z)|}}{3}.
\]
So we only need maximize \(|\det(a,b,c)|\) over vectors
\[
|a|=|b|=1,\qquad |c|=|d|=t,\qquad a+b+c+d=0.
\]

Put \(s=a+b=-(c+d)\), and let \(r=|s|\). Then \(0<r<2\min(1,t)\). Write
\[
a=\frac{s}{2}+p,\qquad b=\frac{s}{2}-p,\qquad
c=-\frac{s}{2}+q,\qquad d=-\frac{s}{2}-q,
\]
where
\[
p\perp s,\quad |p|=\sqrt{1-\frac{r^2}{4}},\qquad
q\perp s,\quad |q|=\sqrt{t^2-\frac{r^2}{4}}.
\]
Thus
\[
|\det(a,b,c)|
\le r\sqrt{1-\frac{r^2}{4}}\sqrt{t^2-\frac{r^2}{4}},
\]
with equality exactly when \(p\perp q\).

Let \(x=r^2/4\). We maximize
\[
2\sqrt{x(1-x)(t^2-x)}.
\]
Equivalently maximize
\[
g(x)=x(1-x)(t^2-x)
\]
on \(0<x<\min(1,t^2)\). Now
\[
g'(x)=3x^2-2(1+t^2)x+t^2,
\]
so the unique interior maximum occurs at
\[
x=\frac{1+t^2-\sqrt{t^4-t^2+1}}{3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|\det(a,b,c)|_{\max}=2\sqrt{x(1-x)(t^2-x)},
\]
and hence
\[
V_{\max}
=\frac{\sqrt{2|\det(a,b,c)|_{\max}}}{3}
=\frac{2}{3}\bigl(x(1-x)(t^2-x)\bigr)^{1/4}.
\]

Equality forces the same value of \(r\), the decompositions above, and \(p\perp q\). Up to an orthogonal transformation and swapping equal-area faces, this determines the four face-area vectors uniquely. Since the face-area vectors determine the tetrahedron uniquely up to congruence, the maximizing tetrahedron is unique up to congruence.
